title: Checks for items declared after some statement in a block.
summary: Items live for the entire scope they are declared in. But statements are processed in order. This might cause confusion as it’s hard to figure out which item is meant in a statement. Clippy puts this lint in the pedantic group, at the level allow.

title: Triggers if an item is declared after the testing module marked with #[cfg(test)].
summary: Having items declared after the testing module is confusing and may lead to bad test coverage. Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for the use of .cloned().collect() on slice to create a Vec.
summary: .to_vec() is clearer Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for the use of .iter().count().
summary: .len() is more efficient and more readable. Clippy puts this lint in the complexity group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for usage of .filter(Result::is_ok) that may be replaced with a .flatten() call.
summary: This lint will require additional changes to the follow-up calls as it affects the type. This pattern is often followed by manual unwrapping of Result. The simplification results in more readable and succinct code without the need for manual unwrapping. Clippy puts this lint in the pedantic group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for usage of .filter(Option::is_some) that may be replaced with a .flatten() call.
summary: This lint will require additional changes to the follow-up calls as it affects the type. This pattern is often followed by manual unwrapping of the Option. The simplification results in more readable and succinct code without the need for manual unwrapping. Clippy puts this lint in the pedantic group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for iterating a map (HashMap or BTreeMap) and ignoring either the keys or values.
summary: Readability. There are keys and values methods that can be used to express that we only need the keys or the values. Clippy puts this lint in the complexity group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for loops on x.next().
summary: next() returns either Some(value) if there was a value, or None otherwise. The insidious thing is that Option<_> implements IntoIterator, so that possibly one value will be iterated, leading to some hard to find bugs. No one will want to write such code except to win an Underhanded Rust Contest. Clippy puts this lint in the correctness group, at the level deny.

title: Checks for usage of iter().next() or iter_mut().next() on a Slice or an Array
summary: These can be shortened into .first() or .first_mut() Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Detects methods named iter or iter_mut that do not have a return type that implements Iterator.
summary: Methods named iter or iter_mut conventionally return an Iterator. Clippy puts this lint in the pedantic group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for usage of .iter().nth()/.iter_mut().nth() on standard library types that have equivalent .get()/.get_mut() methods.
summary: .get() and .get_mut() are equivalent but more concise. Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for the use of iter.nth(0).
summary: iter.next() is equivalent to iter.nth(0), as they both consume the next element, but is more readable. Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for calls to iter, iter_mut or into_iter on empty collections
summary: It is simpler to use the empty function from the standard library: Clippy puts this lint in the nursery group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for calls to iter, iter_mut or into_iter on collections containing a single item
summary: It is simpler to use the once function from the standard library: Clippy puts this lint in the nursery group, at the level allow.

title: Looks for iterator combinator calls such as .take(x) or .skip(x) where x is greater than the amount of items that an iterator will produce.
summary: Taking or skipping more items than there are in an iterator either creates an iterator with all items from the original iterator or an iterator with no items at all. This is most likely not what the user intended to do. Clippy puts this lint in the suspicious group, at the level warn.

title: This is a restriction lint which prevents the use of hash types (i.e., HashSet and HashMap) in for loops.
summary: Because hash types are unordered, when iterated through such as in a for loop, the values are returned in an undefined order. As a result, on redundant systems this may cause inconsistencies and anomalies. In addition, the unknown order of the elements may reduce readability or introduce other undesired side effects. Clippy puts this lint in the restriction group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for usage of _.cloned().<func>() where call to .cloned() can be postponed.
summary: It’s often inefficient to clone all elements of an iterator, when eventually, only some of them will be consumed. Clippy puts this lint in the perf group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for usage of .skip(x).next() on iterators.
summary: .nth(x) is cleaner Clippy puts this lint in the style group, at the level warn.

title: Checks for usage of .skip(0) on iterators.
summary: This was likely intended to be .skip(1) to skip the first element, as .skip(0) does nothing. If not, the call should be removed. Clippy puts this lint in the correctness group, at the level deny.

title: Checks for usage of .drain(..) on Vec and VecDeque for iteration.
summary: .into_iter() is simpler with better performance. Clippy puts this lint in the nursery group, at the level allow.

title: Looks for iter and iter_mut methods without an associated IntoIterator for (&|&mut) Type implementation.
summary: It’s not bad, but having them is idiomatic and allows the type to be used in for loops directly (for val in &iter {}), without having to first call iter() or iter_mut(). Clippy puts this lint in the pedantic group, at the level allow.

title: Checks for calling .step_by(0) on iterators which panics.
summary: This very much looks like an oversight. Use panic!() instead if you actually intend to panic. Clippy puts this lint in the correctness group, at the level deny.
